descs.t: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal crisis: riot police were deployed at the court in Warsaw as Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki clashed over who controls it. Tusk calls it an attack on the rule of law by PiS and Presidents Duda and Nawrocki, while Nawrocki calls the overnight move a forcible takeover. We walk through what happened, in order, and what each side claims.

Donald Tusk says he is defending the rule of law in Poland. President Karol Nawrocki calls the overnight move on the Constitutional Tribunal a forcible takeover and a threat to internal security, and Poland's top court has accused Tusk of staging a coup, The Telegraph reports. We weigh both claims, the police union's open letter, and what this fight means for the rule of law in Poland.

Riot police at Poland's highest court, a president calling it a forcible takeover, and a prime minister warning against giving in to lawlessness and violence. Donald Tusk and Karol Nawrocki are locked in a fight over the Constitutional Tribunal, and the police union says no officer wants to be part of political games. We break down each side's claim, the evidence behind it, and why every free nation should care when a court becomes the battlefield.

intro.plain: Big story out of Poland today. Riot police were deployed at the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw as Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki fight over who controls the court. Tusk calls it an attack on the rule of law by PiS. Nawrocki calls it a forcible takeover. And the police union says officers want no part in political games. So tell me in the chat: who do you believe here?
intro.mid: Straight to Poland, because this one matters for every democracy. Poland's top court has accused Donald Tusk of staging a coup, The Telegraph reports, after riot police were deployed at the Constitutional Tribunal. Tusk says he is defending the rule of law against PiS and President Nawrocki. Nawrocki calls it a threat to internal security. Chat, my question: when two elected leaders both claim the law, who should decide?
intro.bold: Riot police at a country's highest court. That is Poland right now. President Karol Nawrocki calls it a forcible takeover, Donald Tusk calls it defending the rule of law, and the police union says no officer wants to be part of political games. When courts become the battlefield, freedom is what gets hurt. So chat, be honest: is this a coup, or a cleanup?

hook.plain: Riot police deployed at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, and a president and a prime minister each saying the other is breaking the law. Here is what happened, and what each side actually claims.
hook.mid: Poland's top court has accused Donald Tusk of a coup. Tusk says he is saving the rule of law. In the next few minutes, you will see the evidence for each claim.
hook.bold: A president reportedly almost blocked from landing in his own capital. Riot police at the highest court. Poland is in a constitutional crisis, and here is why every free country should be paying attention.

descs.t: Mojtaba Khamenei, the Islamic Republic's Supreme Leader, has ordered the regime's military to answer any threat with no geographic limits and to bring US and Israeli assets within striking range. An AP analysis finds regime strikes damaged or destroyed US air defenses, aircraft and buildings on over two dozen Middle East bases. We walk through the order, the damage count and the talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

The Islamic Republic's new orders from Mojtaba Khamenei come as reports say the US is preparing to resume bombing, possibly as early as Sunday or Monday. A Wall Street Journal examination counts 274 damaged structures at 24 installations, and the Pentagon puts the damage at up to $15 billion. We look at what each side is signalling and what the Hormuz talks could change.

Mojtaba Khamenei is threatening US targets as far away as Europe while his regime offers to reopen the Strait of Hormuz only if the US accepts its conditions. With Washington and Israel reported to be preparing a new bombing campaign, the regime is raising the stakes for everyone. We break down the threat, the damage so far, and what the next days could bring.

descs.t: Alaska's Senate race between Sen. Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola is now a fight over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, the one critics call Decoy Dan. Reports say Peltola's former campaign manager stated under oath that the campaign sought out a Dan Sullivan on the voter rolls, and Sullivan accuses her of lying about what she knew. We walk through the allegations, the lawsuits, and what Alaska's officials say.

President Trump wants ballots in Alaska's Senate race set aside over the alleged Decoy Dan scheme, but attorneys for Alaska call the demand meritless and not possible, AP reports. Democrats argue it would violate the right to a secret vote, while Sen. Dan Sullivan says Mary Peltola lied to Alaskans. We break down the legal fight and what it could mean for the result.

Two men named Dan Sullivan on one Senate ballot, and a sworn statement, reports say, that Mary Peltola's campaign went looking for the second one. Sen. Dan Sullivan calls her denial an absolute lie, Trump wants ballots set aside, and Alaska's own Republican led government says his case is meritless. We dig into what is alleged, what is proven, and what it means for every voter who trusts the name on the ballot.

descs.t: Paris riots: a rioter hurled a firebomb into a police line and it exploded on an officer, setting the officer's shield and helmet alight, as Molotov cocktails and tear gas filled streets near Boulevard Poniatowski and Porte de Charenton. A soldier with a rifle stood guard at Sacré-Cœur on Halloween night. We walk through what happened and what is known about who is behind the violence.

Firebombs are hitting police lines in Paris again, with one officer engulfed in flames on video, and critics say officials still call these marches student protests. Riot police have used tear gas as fires broke out across the city. We look at the escalation, the claims about who is throwing the firebombs, and the pressure now on President Macron.

A Molotov cocktail exploded on a Paris police officer and covered the shield and helmet in flames, and it was not the only firebomb thrown at police lines. Throwing firebombs at police is not protest, and the officers holding the line are paying for it. We break down the attacks, the soldier now guarding the gates of Sacré-Cœur, and what France must do to restore order.

descs.t: President Trump says Flávio Bolsonaro, the right wing candidate who lost Brazil's presidential election to Lula, can stay in the US as long as he wants, Reuters reports. Bolsonaro left Brazil days after the vote, and Trump says he has no plans to meet him. We walk through Trump's comments, Lula's re-election, and how Brazil is reacting.

Trump called Brazil's election a disgrace and said Flávio Bolsonaro was treated very shabbily, but some Bolsonaro supporters had hoped he would go further on their fraud claims, The Economist reports. With Lula re-elected and Bolsonaro now in the US, we look at what Trump's welcome means for Brazil, for Bolsonaro, and for relations between the two countries.

Flávio Bolsonaro lost to Lula, left Brazil a few days later, and now Donald Trump says he can stay in America as long as he wants. Trump calls the election a disgrace, while reports say Brazil is not happy. We break down what happened, what Bolsonaro's supporters claim, and what it means when a defeated candidate looks for his future abroad.

intro.plain: Let's go to Brazil. Flávio Bolsonaro lost the presidential election to Lula, left the country a few days later, and now President Trump says he can stay in the US as long as he wants.
